vignette:
Arthur had been a physician in the same mid-sized North American city for more than thirty years when the bombing happened, and the fact that it occurred during an ordinary workday made it hard for him to ever again trust ordinary days. He was on a commuter bus heading toward the hospital, half-reading lab results on his phone, when the blast shattered the windows and threw passengers into chaos. In the seconds after the explosion, what stayed with him was not just the noise but the shouting, the sharpness of commands, and the sight of people moving with a kind of violent, uncontained panic that he had never imagined on a public bus. He survived, but he came away convinced that the life he had known had been destroyed in a single morning. Since then, Arthur has spoken about the world as if it were fundamentally treacherous, saying with grim certainty that people are not what they seem and that danger can appear anywhere, even in a routine ride across town.

Over time, those beliefs began to shape everything he noticed. When a colleague raised her voice in the emergency department, or when a driver barked instructions at passengers, Arthur felt the same cold tightening he had felt in the bus moments before the blast. Violence in the form of sudden aggression or even the hint of it pulled him back into the conviction that catastrophe could erupt without warning. He began to connect each such moment to the larger story he told himself about the attack: if a city bus, a workplace corridor, or a crowded intersection could become lethal in an instant, then the world truly was dangerous and people could not be trusted. Those appraisals were not abstract for him; they were immediate and personal, and they seemed to confirm themselves every time he was confronted with forcefulness, authority, or the sight of conflict in public.

As the months passed, the same beliefs drove a more guarded way of living. Arthur became vigilant inside his own home, listening for the sounds that might mean someone was entering, checking the lock more than once, and remaining on guard long after the doors were shut. He described himself as irritable and quick to anger, a man who could no longer tolerate minor frustrations without feeling as if he had to defend himself. He was certain that this constant alertness was the only thing keeping him safe. Yet it also kept reinforcing the sense that his life had been altered beyond repair: if he had to monitor every creak in the house and every stranger's expression, then the trauma had not simply happened to him, it had taken over his future. That sense of a destroyed life fed the vigilance further, leaving him more watchful, more suspicious, and more convinced that even familiar places could no longer be taken for granted.

The triggers did not remain confined to memories of the blast itself. Bus riding became especially fraught because it placed him back in the position of a captive passenger, unable to control who sat nearby or where the vehicle might stop. Being given orders or instructions, even in benign settings, could bring a jolt of anger and dread, as if authority itself carried the threat of another unseen disaster. Violence in the news, at work, or on the street had the same effect. Each time one of these reminders appeared, it seemed to Arthur to confirm his belief that the world was dangerous and that people were not what they seemed, and that confirmation made him even more guarded at home and in public. He found himself scanning faces, listening for sudden changes in tone, and mentally rehearsing what he would do if something went wrong. The more he monitored, the more certain he became that danger was everywhere; the more certain he became, the more sharply he reacted to the next reminder.

By the time he came for help, Arthur's life had narrowed in ways his wife had noticed before he would admit them himself. He still worked as a doctor, but he had begun avoiding buses and arranging his schedule around private transport whenever possible, and even then he remained tense on the way to the hospital. At home he was tired from listening for sounds that might mean someone entering, and he hated how easily he became angry with people he loved. What finally brought him to treatment was the fear that this watchfulness was becoming permanent, that he would spend the rest of his life trapped inside the ruins of what had happened to him. More than anything, Arthur hoped to find a way to feel safe enough to stop guarding every door and every passing face, but he was afraid that the bombing had changed him so completely that he no longer knew how.
